question: A WooCommerce Extension Update Broke My Site — How Do I Recover?
metaDescription: Roll back to the previous version first to restore function, then investigate the new version's changelog before attempting to update again.
shortAnswer: Rolling back to the previously working version is the fastest way to restore a functioning site — most plugins (including many premium WooCommerce extensions) support downgrading, either through a rollback feature in a plugin manager, or by manually reinstalling a previous version file. Once the site is stable again, investigate the new version's changelog and any support forum reports before attempting the update again, ideally on staging first.

bodyHtml:
Why Rollback Is Usually the Right First Move

An update that broke the site clearly changed something, and the fastest way to eliminate that change is reverting to the version that was working before — this restores function immediately while a proper investigation into the new version's issue happens separately, rather than leaving the site broken during a longer debugging process.

How to Roll Back

  • Many plugins support version rollback directly through their own settings or through a dedicated "WP Rollback"-style plugin, which lets you select and reinstall a specific previous version without manual file handling.
  • Premium/paid extensions often provide previous version downloads through the vendor's own account portal, since they aren't listed on the public WordPress.org repository.
  • Manual rollback via FTP (replacing the plugin folder with a backed-up previous version) works as a fallback if no rollback tool is available, provided a backup of the previous version exists.
  • A recent full site backup (files and database) is the most reliable rollback method if available, restoring everything to a known-good state at once rather than handling the plugin individually.

After Restoring Function

  1. Check the plugin's changelog and support forum for other users reporting the same issue with the new version, which often surfaces a known fix or workaround.
  2. Report the issue to the plugin's support if it isn't already documented, including specific error details from debug logs.
  3. Test the update again on a staging copy once a fix is available or enough time has passed for the vendor to address it, rather than reattempting blindly on live.
  4. Take a full backup before any future plugin update to make this recovery process faster if it happens again.
